title: The vocative, and the five cases together

objectives.can: Recognise a vocative and distinguish all five cases of a first- or second-declension noun.

explanation.summary: The vocative is the fifth case, the case of calling or addressing someone. It is rare, but it is easy to recognise, and learning it lets you sort every first- and second-declension noun into one of five cases.

sections.heading: Calling someone by name
body: When a speaker turns to a person and speaks to them, the word that names the person is in the vocative. It stands outside the grammar of the rest of the clause: it is not the subject, the object or anything else that the verb governs. In Luke 6:46 Jesus says Κύριε κύριε to his hearers; in Matthew 8:19 a scribe says Διδάσκαλε to Jesus. Often the speaker's words are set off by a comma, and the vocative may come first, in the middle or last.

The vocative is the least frequent of the five cases. In the New Testament it is mostly found in speech, in prayers, in letters (ἀδελφοί, 'brothers', is the commonest address in Paul) and in the Gospels.

sections.heading: How the vocative looks
body: Most of the time the vocative looks exactly like the nominative. This is always so in the plural, and in the singular of the neuter and of most feminine nouns. So ἀδελφοί in 1 Corinthians 1:10 is a vocative plural, but the very same spelling is also the nominative plural; only the sentence tells you which is meant.

The one regular change is in the singular of masculine nouns of the second declension in -ος: the ending becomes -ε. So κύριος gives κύριε, διδάσκαλος gives διδάσκαλε, and υἱός gives υἱέ. A few other nouns have their own vocative, such as γύναι from γυνή, 'woman', and πάτερ from πατήρ, 'father'. These two belong to the third declension, which comes later; learn them now as common forms.

Sometimes a nominative form, with or without the article, is used where one might expect a vocative; θεός is a well-known case. When you meet a nominative form that is plainly speaking to someone, read it as an address.

sections.heading: All five cases together
body: You now have the five cases of Greek. Taking a second-declension noun such as λόγος, the five singular endings are -ος (nominative), -ου (genitive), -ῳ (dative), -ον (accusative) and -ε (vocative); the plural endings are -οι, -ων, -οις, -ους and -οι. The paradigms below are filled in from the New Testament and from the other texts of the library. A dash means that the form is not found in the texts, not that it does not exist: the vocative singular of λόγος, for example, would be formed on the same pattern as κύριε, but the library holds no example, so the table leaves it out.

Two habits make parsing quicker. First, look at the article if there is one: it usually settles case, number and gender at once. Second, remember which cases can be mistaken for each other: the plural vocative and nominative are the same; the dative and the genitive of the second declension differ only by an iota subscript or a circumflex; and a neuter noun has one form for nominative, accusative and vocative.

sections.heading: What each case is doing
body: In short: the nominative names the subject (and what is said about the subject after 'is'); the accusative usually names the object; the genitive usually shows 'of', possession or source; the dative usually shows 'to', 'for', 'by' or 'in'; and the vocative addresses someone. These are first descriptions. Each case has more uses than this, and the preposition in front of a noun often decides which use is meant.

misunderstandings: The vocative is not a case of grammar inside the clause. A word in the vocative is not the subject, even though it may name a person who is mentioned in the sentence.
ἀδελφοί is not always 'the brothers do something'. When it stands in a comma-marked address, as in Paul's letters, it is a vocative plural, 'brothers!'.
Not every address ends in -ε. Plurals, neuters and most feminine nouns keep the nominative spelling, and a few nouns, such as πατήρ, have an irregular vocative.

deeper.heading: An old case, kept in a small corner
body: Grammarians have often said that the vocative is not really a case at all, because it does not relate a noun to a verb or another noun. Greek grammars still count it among the cases because some nouns have a special ending for it. Where an adjective goes with a vocative noun, it may be in the vocative or in the nominative form; the next lesson takes up adjectives.
